title: Giving a benign result to an anxious patient

header.contentArea: Communicating good news well after a cancer history
guidelineVersions: GMC: Good Medical Practice (In effect 30 January 2024)
NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer (Published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025)

related.why: The examination and assessment that led to this result
An earlier results conversation this one contrasts with in tone

brief.scenario: Ms Linford's triple assessment for her new lump confirms a fibroadenoma, a benign finding.
brief.task: Give her this result. You have 7 minutes.
brief.note: Good news is easy to under-deliver: rushing it, or failing to address the anxiety that led up to it, can leave a patient unsettled even after a reassuring result.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Give the result clearly and promptly, but don't assume good news needs no space - check how the waiting period has felt and address any lingering worry directly.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating a benign result as needing no discussion beyond the headline, when the anxiety leading up to it may not resolve immediately just because the news is good.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I've got good news for you today."

flow: Check how the waiting period has been
Explain what a fibroadenoma is and what it means going forward
Confirm ongoing surveillance plan and closing

grid.label: Checking in before the result
grid.fail: Delivers the result without acknowledging the wait she's had.
grid.pass: Briefly checks how the waiting period has felt for her before giving the result.
grid.high: Recognises this wait may have felt especially anxious given her personal history, without assuming this specific patient's reaction.

grid.label: Delivering the result
grid.fail: Delays or buries the good news behind unnecessary preamble.
grid.pass: States clearly and promptly that the result is benign, a fibroadenoma.
grid.high: Delivers this warmly and directly, matching the tone appropriately to good news rather than defaulting to a serious, guarded delivery style.

grid.label: Explaining the finding
grid.fail: Cannot explain what a fibroadenoma is.
grid.pass: Explains simply that a fibroadenoma is a common, benign breast lump made of fibrous and glandular tissue, not cancer.
grid.high: Explains it in a way that reduces, rather than adds to, medical uncertainty for her (e.g. addressing whether it needs removal or will change).

grid.label: Addressing lingering anxiety
grid.fail: Assumes the good news alone resolves all her anxiety and closes the conversation.
grid.pass: Checks explicitly whether she still has any worries despite the reassuring result.
grid.high: Validates that anxiety can persist even after good news, especially given her history, without pathologising this reaction.

grid.label: Ongoing plan
grid.fail: Does not mention what happens with this lump or her ongoing surveillance going forward.
grid.pass: Confirms whether the lump needs any monitoring or intervention, and that her existing surveillance plan continues as before.
grid.high: Distinguishes clearly between monitoring this specific benign lump (if needed) and her separate, ongoing cancer surveillance plan, so she isn't confused between the two.

grid.label: Closing
grid.fail: Ends abruptly without checking her understanding or offering further contact.
grid.pass: Checks her understanding and confirms how to get in touch if any further worries or new symptoms arise.
grid.high: Ends warmly, acknowledging this must be a relief after the wait, without being dismissive of the anxiety it caused.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Results are fine, it's a fibroadenoma, nothing to worry about, see you next year.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: So I don't need to worry about it at all?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, that's it, you're all done.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How has the wait for these results been for you?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Honestly, pretty stressful, given everything before.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I've got good news - the lump is a fibroadenoma, which is benign.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A fibroadenoma is a common, non-cancerous lump made of normal breast tissue, and it doesn't usually need removing unless it's causing problems.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Even with good news like this, do you still have any worries or questions?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I think I'll just feel anxious about every lump from now on, if I'm honest.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's a really understandable response given what you've been through. Your ongoing cancer surveillance plan continues exactly as before - this result doesn't change that.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Do you have any other questions, and you know how to reach us if anything else comes up?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How has this wait been for you, especially given everything you've already been through?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm glad I can put your mind at ease - the lump is a fibroadenoma, and that's benign, not cancer.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: [Tearful with relief.] I can't tell you what that means to hear.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A fibroadenoma is a really common, harmless kind of lump made of ordinary breast tissue - it doesn't need to be removed unless it grows or becomes uncomfortable, and it isn't linked to your previous cancer.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Even with a reassuring result like this, it's completely normal if the anxiety doesn't just switch off - do you still have any worries you'd like to talk through?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I think I'll worry about every new lump now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's a very natural response after what you've been through, not something to feel bad about. Just to be clear - this doesn't change your existing cancer surveillance plan at all, that continues exactly as scheduled, separate from this finding.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This must be a real relief after the wait you've had. Do you have everything you need, and do you know how to reach us if anything worries you before your next scheduled check?

failures.move: Assuming a benign result automatically resolves all anxiety.
failures.consequence: Dismisses a genuine, often persistent, psychological response to breast symptoms after a cancer history, leaving her unsupported despite good clinical news.

failures.move: Not distinguishing between monitoring the benign lump and her separate ongoing cancer surveillance.
failures.consequence: Risks confusion about what follow-up, if any, is still needed and why.

failures.move: Delivering the result with no acknowledgement of how difficult the waiting period may have been.
failures.consequence: Misses an opportunity to validate a genuinely stressful experience, even though the outcome was reassuring.

failures.move: Delays or buries the good news behind unnecessary preamble.
failures.consequence: Prolongs her anxiety longer than necessary when the news is actually reassuring.

failures.move: Cannot explain what a fibroadenoma actually is.
failures.consequence: Leaves her with a label but no understanding of why it isn't a threat.

recovery.when: You moved on too quickly after good news
recovery.line: Even though this is good news, I want to check in properly - how are you feeling about it?

recovery.when: You didn't clarify her ongoing surveillance plan
recovery.line: I should be clear - this doesn't affect your existing follow-up plan, which continues as scheduled.

knowledge.fact: A fibroadenoma is a common benign breast lesion composed of fibrous and glandular tissue and does not require removal unless symptomatic or enlarging.
Anxiety after a benign result can persist in patients with a personal history of breast cancer, and acknowledging this is part of good communication, distinct from the clinical result itself.
A benign finding on a new lump does not alter a patient's separate, ongoing risk-based cancer surveillance schedule.

recall.think: Good news still deserves space; anxiety doesn't switch off with reassurance; keep this result separate from her ongoing surveillance plan.
recall.say: "It's completely normal if the anxiety doesn't just switch off."
do: Acknowledge the waiting period, then deliver good news clearly and warmly
Check for lingering anxiety rather than assuming it's resolved
Clarify that ongoing surveillance is unaffected by this benign finding

numbers.meaning: interval of her ongoing BRCA2-tailored mammographic surveillance, unaffected by this benign finding

recall.trap: Assuming a benign result needs no further discussion or emotional acknowledgement.
recall.finish: A clearly delivered benign result, acknowledged anxiety, and clarity on her unchanged ongoing surveillance plan.

partner.opening: Please give this patient her results. You have 7 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 45, back for results after a stressful wait. The result is benign (fibroadenoma), which is a huge relief, but you suspect you'll feel anxious about every future lump given your history.

reveals.trigger: Candidate checks how the wait has felt
reveals.finding: You reveal the wait has been very stressful, with poor sleep.

reveals.trigger: Candidate checks for lingering anxiety after the good news
reveals.finding: You admit you think you'll worry about every future lump.

reveals.trigger: Candidate clarifies her ongoing surveillance is unaffected
reveals.finding: You feel clearer about what happens next.

push.question: Does this mean I don't need to come back for my usual checks?
push.expect: Clarify that her existing surveillance plan is unchanged and separate from this benign finding.

push.question: Will I always be this anxious about new lumps?
push.expect: Validate this as a common and understandable response, without pathologising it, and offer support if it feels overwhelming.

curveballs.prompt: Can you just remove it anyway, so I don't have to think about it?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that removal isn't clinically necessary for an asymptomatic fibroadenoma, discuss her reasoning, and offer to talk through her anxiety rather than simply agreeing to unnecessary surgery.

curveballs.prompt: I don't think I believe it's really benign.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge this feeling without dismissing it, reassure her about how the diagnosis was reached (triple assessment), and offer to answer any further questions she has about the result.
